books.section: Topic 8.2 The Cold War from 1945 to 1980
America in an Era of Turmoil (1960-1975)
Unit 8: The Postwar Period and Cold War (1945-1980)

primary_sources: John F. Kennedy, address on the Cuban Missile Crisis, October 22, 1962 (paraphrased in the question)

stimulus.source_note: Original summary passage written for this question; facts from the grounding books.
stimulus.text: In October 1962, American reconnaissance photographs showed Soviet missile sites under construction in Cuba, ninety miles from Florida. President John Kennedy announced a naval quarantine of the island and demanded the missiles be removed. For thirteen days the world waited while the two sides negotiated in secret. Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev agreed to withdraw the missiles, and the United States privately promised to remove its missiles from Turkey.

source: original; stimulus is an original summary passage written for this question
stem: Kennedy's choice of a naval quarantine rather than an air strike on the missile sites best shows which concern?

options.text: Kennedy wanted to avoid alerting the American public to the crisis.
options.misconception: Kennedy announced the crisis on television; he did not hide it from the public.

options.text: The navy was the only military force available to the United States in 1962.
options.misconception: An air strike was on the table and debated; the quarantine was chosen over it.

options.text: Kennedy wanted to give Khrushchev time and room to withdraw without forcing a war.
The Soviet missiles in Cuba were not yet a threat to the United States.
options.misconception: Missiles ninety miles from Florida were a real threat; that is why Kennedy demanded their removal.

rationales.A: Kennedy told the public himself in a televised address on October 22, 1962. Alerting the public was part of his plan, not something he avoided.
rationales.B: The United States had bombers, troops, and missiles ready in 1962, and an air strike was seriously debated. The navy was a choice, not the only option.
rationales.C: A quarantine stopped Soviet ships without firing on Cuba, and it left days for secret talks. Background from the books: Kennedy's advisers feared an air strike would kill Soviet soldiers and force Khrushchev to answer with war.
rationales.D: The missiles could strike most of the United States, which is why Kennedy acted at all. A threat that was not yet real would not have produced a thirteen-day crisis.
rationales.general:
1. An air strike would have killed Soviet soldiers on the first day and left Khrushchev little choice but to answer.
2. A quarantine stopped ships at sea instead, which put pressure on Moscow without firing a shot.
3. That pause gave secret talks time to work, and the missiles came out without a war.
Remember: In a crisis, the best first move is often the one that leaves the other side a way out.
